propositions: اختتم في مدينة حلب السورية معرض المهن الحرفية والتراثية القديمة، الذي أُقيم تحت شعار "لكل حرفة تاريخ يُروى"، بمشاركة حرفيين وفنانين وأصحاب مشروعات سعوا إلى إحياء الحرف المهددة بالاندثار، وتطوير منتجاتها بما يجمع بين الأصالة والحداثة، ونقل خبراتها إلى الأجيال الجديدة.

وجاء المعرض في إطار مشروع "صون"، الذي ركز على المهن التراثية الحلبية، بهدف الحفاظ على هذا الإرث الثقافي غير المادي، وتعريف الأجيال الجديدة بالحرف القديمة التي ارتبطت بتاريخ المدينة وحياة سكانها، فضلا عن مساعدة العاملين فيها على تطوير مشروعاتهم وتحويل مهاراتهم التقليدية إلى فرص عمل مستدامة.

وقالت مديرة المشروع روميسة شيخ، إن العمل بدأ باستقطاب المستفيدين وفق معايير محددة، مع تخصيص النسبة الكبرى من المشاركين للنساء، مقابل 20% للرجال، بهدف مساعدة النساء اللواتي يمارسن الحرف التراثية في المنازل على الانتقال إلى ريادة الأعمال، وتوسيع نطاق أعمالهن لتصل إلى الأسواق.

وأوضحت أن المشاركات خضعن لدورات تدريبية تناولت التسويق والتسعير الرقمي، وآليات ترخيص المشروعات، وبناء هوية بصرية مميزة لكل مشروع، بما يساعد صاحبات الحرف على تقديم منتجاتهن بصورة أكثر احترافية والوصول إلى شرائح أوسع من الزبائن.

وأضافت شيخ أن المشروع نظم جولات في أسواق حلب القديمة للتعرف إلى تاريخ الحرف وطبيعة ممارستها، قبل إقامة المعرض الختامي على مدى 3 ليال، في موقع اُختير بمحيط قلعة حلب ، بما يتناسب مع الهوية التاريخية للمكان وطبيعة المبادرة التي تمحورت حول التراث وسبل الحفاظ عليه.
وتراوحت أعمار المشاركين بين 17 و60 عاما، في دلالة على اهتمام فئات عمرية مختلفة بالحرف التقليدية، ورغبة أجيال جديدة في تعلمها وتطويرها.

ومن بين المشاركين في المعرض الفنان التشكيلي والنحات على الخشب أحمد هنداوي الذي عمل على إحياء هذه الحرفة التي باتت مهددة بالاندثار، من خلال إدخالها إلى مجالي الديكور والخط العربي، وتقديم أعمال جمعت بين التقنيات التقليدية واللمسات الفنية الحديثة.

وأوضح هنداوي أنه سعى إلى نقل النحت على الخشب من الاستخدامات التقليدية المرتبطة بالأثاث إلى إنتاج قطع فنية يمكن اقتناؤها بوصفها لوحات تزين المنازل، بما يمنح الحرفة أبعادا جمالية جديدة ويسهم في الحفاظ على جانب من تراث حلب الصناعي والفني.

وأشار إلى أن المدينة كانت رائدة في مجال النحت على الخشب خلال الفترة الممتدة من سبعينيات القرن الماضي إلى تسعينياته، معربا عن أمله في استعادة هذه المكانة، ليس من خلال إقامة المعارض فحسب، بل عبر إنشاء أماكن متخصصة لتعليم الحرفة وتحويلها إلى مادة دراسية أو منهج تدريبي يتيح للشباب تعلمها وتطويرها وإضافة أفكار جديدة إليها.
بدورها، عرضت الحرفية المتخصصة في المكرمية رغد وزان تجربتها في تطوير هذه الحرفة التراثية وتوسيع استخداماتها.
وأوضحت أن المكرمية ارتبطت تاريخيا بصناعة شبكات الصيد لدى البحارة، الذين كانوا يستغلون رحلاتهم الطويلة في إنجاز قطع يدوية، فيما اشتهرت في حلب باستخدامها في صناعة حاملات النباتات.

وقالت رغد إنها عملت على تطوير منتجات المكرمية لتشمل الديكورات والمستلزمات المنزلية المتنوعة، وإعادة إدخالها إلى البيوت الحلبية، لما تمنحه من إحساس بالدفء والنعومة، فضلا عن تعريف الشباب والأطفال بتاريخ الحرفة وتشجيعهم على ابتكار تصاميم جديدة مستوحاة منها.
وأبدت إحدى زائرات المعرض اعتزازها باستمرار الحرف اليدوية في المدينة، بعدما اعتقد كثيرون أنها مهددة بالاختفاء، مشيدة بالدعم الذي يحظى به الحرفيون وبالدقة الفنية التي ظهرت في المنتجات المعروضة.

وقالت إن النحت على الخشب كان من أبرز الأعمال التي لفتت انتباهها، لما يتسم به من دقة وتفاصيل فنية تعكس روح الحرفي الذي أنجز القطعة، معربة عن أملها أن تصل المنتجات التراثية الحلبية إلى الأسواق الخارجية، بما يعزز حضور المدينة بوصفها مركزا عريقا للحرف والأصالة.

وشكل المعرض مساحة لعرض المهارات التقليدية أمام الجمهور، وفرصة لربط الحرفيين بالأسواق الحديثة، في محاولة للحفاظ على الموروث الحرفي الحلبي وضمان استمراره عبر الأجيال، مع تطويره بما يتناسب مع متطلبات الحياة المعاصرة.
I write anonymously on behalf of hundreds of desperate farmers whose livelihoods have been impaired due to the construction of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway.
Months ago, officials cleared our farms, destroying our cocoa, food crops and oil palms.
We stepped aside willingly because we were promised prompt, fair compensation.
While the media recently reported that a first tranche of payments was made to over 450 farmers, a massive, forgotten number of us have received absolutely nothing.
Our lands are gone, we have no alternative incomes, and our children's school fees are due.
When we try to ask for updates, we are met with total silence.
The Ministry of Roads and Highways, the Ghana Highway Authority and the Land Valuation Division have become completely unreachable.
Development should not destroy the citizens it claims to serve.
You cannot take a farmer’s only source of survival and abandon them.
We appeal to the media to investigate this delay.
We urge the Minister of Roads and Highways and the project coordinators to break their silence and immediately publish a clear, transparent payment schedule for those of us left behind.
Alexus Grynkewich aims to send a clear signal to the Kremlin that the alliance will resist any attack.
NATO’s top commander U.S.

Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere.

Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade .

“Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”
The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia.

It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran .

Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said.

NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.”
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.”
But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.”
The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan.
Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.”
Under Trump, the U.S. has sought to refocus its military on other priorities such as the Indo-Pacific, homeland security and the Western Hemisphere.
U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said in Warsaw on Monday that Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic concerns.
The Pentagon has already cut its contributions to NATO crisis forces and is set to unveil a review of U.S. forces in Europe by the end of the year.
“No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” Grynkewich argued, but added that “ultimately, it's a political decision about who's providing troops where.”

Emma Burrows, Associated Press WARSAW, Poland (AP) — NATO's top military commander said the alliance is "ready to fight tonight" if it is attacked, as European officials warn Russia could test NATO's defenses with increased covert attacks or a limited military incursion.

European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport.
If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S.
General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw Monday.
Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called NATO's "Theory of Victory."

The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings."
Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack NATO is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces.

But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said NATO's combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground.
"My theory of victory is simple," he told the Warsaw conference.

"We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us."
That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said.

In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the NATO alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent.
Denmark's defense intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the NATO alliance.

But, at the same time, President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try lower prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections.

"Ultimately it's a political decision," as to where troops are deployed but "no one should question the U.S. commitment to the alliance," Grynkewich said.
It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a "coherent" response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow "where our red lines are."
The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine.

BELFAST — Despite assuring an audience today that a conflict on NATO territory is neither “imminent or inevitable,” Gen.
Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, outlined a strategic “theory of victory” and offered a warning to potential aggressors.

He told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO’s aim is to deter adversaries, “but if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” adding that “any attack against any ally” will end up “utterly futile.”

NATO is capable of carrying out this vision by implementing its “theory of victory,” a classified version of which was agreed upon by all 32 alliance members “about three months ago,” according to Grynkewich .

Grynkewich, who also serves as commander of United States European Command, did not say against whom, exactly, the alliance would fight, but the speech comes as European capitals have increasingly called out Russia for what they alleged are a string of sabotage cases across the continent.
Grynkewich said the incidents were making allied populations “a bit nervous.”
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of the alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do,” he said.
Grynkewich warned, “I want others to know who might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”
The theory of victory is structured around blocking, blunting and breaking an enemy — beginning with stymieing an initial attack and preventing an enemy advance by weakening it.
Drawing on the final part of the theory, said Grynkewich, “we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”

Concentrating more on the warfighting elements to execute the new doctrine, he noted the “synchronized employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level” in order to “overwhelm enemy formations in contact.”
The end result would see enemy forces degraded to such an extent that they would be unable to continue an attack, explained Grynkewich.
“Across the alliance, we’re taking steps to operationalize this theory and maximize the readiness of our forces,” he made clear.
“If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight.”
Grynkewich’s comments come as Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned today that NATO allies must be prepared to deal with a deadly Russian hybrid attack.

Separately, when assessing the state of the Ukraine war, Grynkewich noted that the frontline has “largely stabilized” and that Russian long range attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, “probably” won’t break the will of the country’s civilian population.
Sanaa has come under intense bombing since the Yemeni government announced a campaign to take the capital from the Houthis.

Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023.

The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014.
Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz.
This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties.
An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians.
The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa.
Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again.
Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm , launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes.
Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers.
Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites.
Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents.
“When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera.
“At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.”
On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was.
With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa.

“The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said.

Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people .
Air strikes on Sanaa have killed civilians and sparked fear as the Yemeni government pushes Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake the city from Houthi control.

Kathmandu— Since midnight on Tuesday, air strikes have rattled Yemen’s capital Sanaa after the internationally recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen to seize the city from Houthi forces that have held it since 2014, with the campaign relying on aerial bombardment that has already killed a child, wounded seven civilians and struck the international airport, leaving residents fearful of further attacks and possible displacement.

Air strikes have hit Sanaa repeatedly since the early hours of Tuesday, with an attack on Monday in the Sa’wan area killing a child and wounding seven other civilians, and a separate strike on Sanaa’s international airport killing two workers.

Ghamadan Abood, a 30‑year‑old courier and Sanaa resident, told Al Jazeera that learning of the new operation made his feeling of security shrink, adding that "at any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties."
He also said the strikes could be aimed at military facilities but often lie near neighbourhoods, farms or roads, putting innocent people at risk of death, injury or terror.

Saleh Ayidh, a 50‑year‑old father of five living in Sanaa, said he still views the city as a safe place distant from the front lines, yet warned that no place in Yemen is truly safe and war can spread anywhere, noting that his family would decide whether to leave if the air strikes keep intensifying and that without safety life is hard.

The offensive, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, was announced by the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al‑Alimi, and relies on air power because government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away, engaged in fighting with the Houthis on the west coast and around Taiz.

Raiman al‑Hamdani, a London‑based Yemen analyst, told Al Jazeera that while government forces look strong on paper they are scattered across multiple fronts and equipped with outdated gear, saying they "can hold their lines but can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds."

Fuad Ali, a 40‑year‑old university graduate in Sanaa, said the Saudi‑backed government has lost public trust after failing to seize the coastal Hodeidah province or the Al‑Jawf desert province, questioning how it could recapture mountainous Sanaa; he added that Operation Dawn of Yemen will bring more destruction and increase civilian casualties, but expressed optimism that it will not damage Sanaa as the 2015 Operation Decisive Storm did.

The International Organization for Migration reports that more than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, with the majority fleeing Taiz governorate where the most intense ground fighting between government and Houthi forces has occurred.

Saleh Ayidh said he fears the new air strikes will also force people from their homes in the north, stating that his family will decide whether to leave the city if the strikes keep intensifying and that without safety life is hard.

The UN World Food Programme warned that three‑quarters of families in parts of Yemen are going hungry, and Wafiq Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni‑Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera that rising prices of food and fuel are a real worry for the entire population and will worsen the humanitarian situation.

Residents of Sanaa have begun stockpiling food and fuel, viewing the recent air strikes as a sign that war has returned to the capital; grocery owner Nashwan, 24, said he has boosted his inventory of rice, cheese, milk, biscuits, cooking oil and sugar and bought 100 litres of petrol for his minibus in case a fuel crisis hits.

Nashwan told Al Jazeera that these commodities may become expensive in the coming days and that he does not want to feel the impact of the war immediately, adding that if the war keeps escalating buying them would cost him more.

Analysts note that any road closures or decline in imports caused by the war and a Saudi naval siege on Houthi areas would present major challenges for civilians, with rising food and fuel prices already a real worry for the entire population.

The Saudi‑led coalition said Sanaa, Saada and Amran are among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats and that its ongoing military operations aim to curb the group’s ability to launch missiles into the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people.

Observers draw a parallel to the 2015 Operation Decisive Storm, which caused hundreds of civilian deaths in Sanaa and drew international condemnation, noting that the government and coalition say they have learned lessons from that episode.

Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023.

The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014. list 1 of 3Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis list 2 of 3World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport list 3 of 3Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz.
This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties.
An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians.
The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa.
Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again.
Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm, launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes.
Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers.
Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites.
Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents.
“When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera.
“At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.”
On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was.
With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa.

“The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said.

Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people.
On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said Sanaa, Saada, and Amran were among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats.

Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”
On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to.

Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said.
“It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added.

“It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said.

In October 1901, the Alexandrinsky Russian-Muslim School for Girls — the first Muslim girls’ school in the Caucasus — opened in Baku with funding from oil industrialist and philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev.
Dressed in black, Taghiyev stands in the centre among the pupils and teachers of the Baku Muslim Girls’ School.
New school uniform requirements have once again brought Azerbaijan’s secular tradition into conflict with the religious beliefs of some families.
But behind the dispute over clothing lies a simpler question: how can every girl be kept in education?
In videos shared on social media, schoolgirls wearing headscarves leave school in tears: they have been denied entry to lessons.
The voices of the pupils themselves are heard far less often in the public debate than declarations about their future.
A headscarf alone cannot reveal whether a girl wears it out of personal conviction, family custom or pressure.
Nor can her tears establish every cause of the conflict.
That is why any solution must begin with a conversation with the child, rather than assigning someone else’s position to her.
For some parents, what is happening has already become a question of access to education.
One parent in Sumgayit told AzadlıqRadiosu : “Our children are not being allowed into school because of our religious beliefs.”
This is a parent’s testimony, rather than a fact established by a court.
But it identifies these families’ central fear: a clothing requirement could mean missed lessons.
The current dispute gained fresh momentum following Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309 of September 21, 2026.
It added a prohibition to the school uniform rules on clothing elements that undermine the uniform’s consistency and do not comply with the principle of secular general education.
Yet the word “hijab” does not appear in the document.
Questions of compliance have been assigned to schools’ pedagogical councils , while parents are required to ensure that their children follow the rules.
National dress, or elements of it, may be worn at events dedicated to Azerbaijan’s history and culture with the permission of the pedagogical council.
Azerbaijan's hijab restrictions spark school protests and arrests Anger is growing in Azerbaijan after girls wearing hijabs were barred from schools under new uniform rules.
Students and teachers have staged demonstrations, while dozens have reportedly been arrested and users report disruptions to social media platforms.

Barring schoolgirls who wear the hijab could drive some students out of education, Azerbaijani lawyer Akram Hasanov said, arguing that parents should not automatically be blamed when an adolescent refuses to remove her headscarf.
Hasanov raised the issue in a Facebook post reported by Vesti Baku .
Hasanov described a hypothetical case in which a 14-year-old girl insists on wearing the hijab while her parents urge her to remove it and attend school.
If she refuses, he asked, who should be held responsible for her absence?

He cited Article 181.0.1 of Azerbaijan’s Code of Administrative Offenses, which provides penalties for depriving a child of education: 100 manats for individuals, 300 manats for officials and 5,000 manats for legal entities.
In Hasanov’s view, a parent may be at fault if the parent prevents a child from attending school.
But he said the situation is different when an adolescent independently refuses to attend because she will not remove the headscarf.
He also rejected forced removal of the hijab or physical compulsion, saying such conduct could itself create legal liability.
“Secularism does not mean atheism,” Hasanov wrote, arguing that adolescents can hold religious convictions of their own.
He recalled that after the Jan.
20, 1990, Soviet crackdown in Baku, he removed his Pioneer scarf and protested against the Soviet Union at school before he turned 13, despite pressure from teachers and his parents.
Hasanov warned that excluding girls who hold religious beliefs could alienate them from the state and deprive them of an education.
He also linked the issue to wider debates about family values and demographic concerns.
The central question, he said, is how to keep a student in education when a school requires her to remove the hijab but she refuses to do so.
In Azerbaijan’s schools, a ban on wearing the hijab has led to female students being barred from classes, demands for female teachers to remove their headscarves and protests.
On 12 October, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of 37 people in connection with incidents over compliance with school uniform rules.
As a result, parents demanding that schools allow their children to attend lessons now face criminal proceedings.
The authorities justify the restrictions by citing the need for a uniform school dress code and secular education.
However, the consequences for students barred from classes are tangible: they must give up religious clothing to attend lessons.
At the heart of the dispute is the question of how the state exercises its authority to set school dress code requirements and how these restrictions undermine children’s right to education.
